This patient with known diabetes presents with symptomatic hypoglycemia (glucose 41 mg/dL) and progressive confusion. Common causes in diabetics are medication-related (insulin or sulfonylurea). Workup shows: insulin and C‑peptide reported as “normal” despite concurrent hypoglycemia — which is inappropriately high (insulin should be suppressed when glucose is 41 mg/dL). Beta‑hydroxybutyrate is not elevated, consistent with suppressed ketogenesis from hyperinsulinemia. Sulfonylurea screen is negative and ethanol, cortisol, and liver/renal tests are normal, making sulfonylurea, alcohol intoxication, adrenal insufficiency, and hepatic/renal failure unlikely. A plausible unifying explanation is exogenous (iatrogenic or surreptitious) insulin administration — including insulin analogs that some assays may not reliably detect — causing hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia with suppressed ketones. [DIAGNOSIS]
Acute hypoglycemia due to exogenous (iatrogenic or factitious) insulin administration.
